doc.title: Norman Simmons interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 27, 2007 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Joe Williams and Harry Edison's group and its ego clashes
summary: Joe's group with Sweets had ego conflicts with Jimmy Forrest despite a fine rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: That’s right. After he left Basie and he put this group together with Sweets and them, it was so stressful for him that he did not want to have any more groups.
I’m glad you brought that up. Because I got this, every once in a while I got this feeling or — that the relationship between Joe and Sweets was strained.
It was. Because all these high-powered egos on that stage. Who was the saxophone player at that time? Was it Jimmy —
Jimmy Forrest. You understand what I mean? There was ego conflict. Now the rhythm section was okay I think. You had Junior Mance and Bob Cranshaw and what’s his name out in Philadelphia I think.

No not Jimmy Cobb, out of Philadelphia. But anyway they had a wonderful rhythm section together. As a matter of fact they scared me. Because when I heard them, it’s like you listen to someone play and you say hey, you know, I can do that, or I can do it better. But when I heard them I didn’t think I could do it better.
Mickey Roker. That’s right. And they had it locked down. But the three men, between Joe and Sweets and Jimmy Forrest, that’s where the egos clashed on the front line.
